subject: Failover acceptance, data-lag matrix and timebox discussion
messages:
From: Emily Carter <emily.carter@sterlingbank.com>
To: marissa_cole <marissa.cole@redwood.inference>
Cc: technical.ops@sterlingbank.com, procurement@sterlingbank.com
Date: 2026-10-05T08:14:00-04:00
Subject: Clarification on failover acceptance and RTO/RPO commitments

Marissa,

Thanks for the initial DR package — Sterling's security and ops teams reviewed it and we have a focused set of acceptance criteria to validate in our RFP response. We need clear, testable commitments so we can sign off the risk assessment. Can you confirm the following in a single response: 

- A single-line statement for the maximum RTO you will commit for production inference endpoints during a full-region outage (assume cross-region warm-standby).
- The RPO for customer-facing request data and for internal control-plane metadata (authorization tokens, audit logs).
- Whether KV/prefix cache is preserved across failover or requires warm-up (and expected warm-up time to reach steady-state latency).
- DNS/traffic cutover mechanics (DNS TTL, BGP weights, Route53 health checks, or other) and an approximate timebox for global traffic cutover we can use in our runbook.

Also, please attach a simple "acceptance matrix" we can include in our procurement checklist (we referred to the doc you labeled RTO_RPO_v1 but would prefer the one-page spreadsheet).

We have a sandbox window next Wednesday, 2026-10-13, 09:00-12:00 ET for a dry-run — would Redwood be available?

Thanks,
Emily
Emily Carter
Director, Technical Risk & Resiliency
Sterling Bank

From: marissa_cole <marissa.cole@redwood.inference>
To: Emily Carter <emily.carter@sterlingbank.com>
Cc: vivek_kulkarni@redwood.inference, rishi_malhotra@redwood.inference, grace_oconnor@redwood.inference
Date: 2026-10-05T10:03:00-04:00
Subject: Re: Clarification on failover acceptance and RTO/RPO commitments

Emily — thanks for the clear list. Below are concise, testable answers we propose for inclusion in the acceptance matrix; I also attached a one-page spreadsheet (RTO_RPO_acceptance_matrix_v1.xlsx) and an excerpt from our operational playbook (failover-playbook-extract.pdf).

1) RTO commitment (production inference endpoints): 
- Commitment: 95th-percentile RTO <= 3 minutes (<= 180 seconds) for API traffic when failing over from one region to a pre-provisioned warm-standby region under normal capacity.
- Note: For ultra-low-latency enterprise tiers (Dedicated GPU pools with pinned capacity) we can agree to an operational SLA target of 60s for the control-plane cutover and 95th-percentile 120s for full traffic routing and model load, subject to a reserved-capacity contract.

2) RPO commitments: 
- Customer request/interaction data: RPO = best-effort for ephemeral request data (generated tokens and session KV caches are in-memory and not a persistent store); persistent logs and audit trails are written to S3-compatible object storage with RPO <= 60 seconds (i.e., durable within 60s).
- Control-plane metadata (auth tokens, configuration changes, audit logs): RPO <= 5 seconds for replicated control-plane state using our async replication with durable write-ahead logs.

3) KV/prefix cache behavior: 
- KV and prefix caches are in-memory per-serving node and are not synchronously replicated across regions. After failover, requests will route to the standby region which has cold model weights loaded (pre-warmed per policy) but an empty KV cache.
- Expected warm-up: 5–12 minutes to reach steady-state 95th-percentile latencies for conversational workloads depending on session locality and average prompt length. We mitigate cold-cache impact via: incremental prefetching for pinned prefixes, prioritized warm-up for active customers, and temporary traffic shadowing to populate caches prior to cutover in scheduled drills.

4) Traffic cutover mechanics and timebox: 
- Primary mechanism: Active health-check + DNS with Route53 weighted routing and a low DNS TTL (default 60s) as the standard public recovery path. For customers preferring network-level failover we support BGP anycast (for private connectivity customers) and accelerate cutover using a pre-established edge-route policy.
- Typical cutover timebox: Control-plane failover and routing decision: 30–90 seconds (control-plane-only). Full traffic convergence (including DNS propagation and model instance readiness to target capacity) is expected in 60–180 seconds for hosted customers; add the KV warm-up window above for steady-state latency.

Acceptance criteria (recommended one-liners for the procurement checklist):
- Failover test 1: Initiate region outage; Redwood will restore API availability in the standby region and route production traffic such that 95% of requests succeed within 180s.
- Failover test 2: Control-plane metadata consistency check: audit logs and token revocation status must be visible in standby within 5s of issuance.
- Evidence: runbook excerpt + sample logs (attached: sample-failover-run-logs.zip) and a signed post-test run report.

5) Test availability: We can staff the Wednesday window (2026-10-13 09:00-12:00 ET). We'll need: a list of test endpoints, expected request volume (we recommend starting light: 10–20 rps ramp to 100 rps), and one Redwood SPOC for the run (I'll be lead).

Next steps: Please confirm acceptance wording for the two RTO tiers (hosted vs Dedicated) and confirm the sandbox traffic profile. If that looks good we'll sign the one-page matrix and schedule the runbook dry-run.

Thanks — attaching the spreadsheets now.

Best,
Marissa Cole
Director, Solutions Engineering
Redwood Inference

--

From: Vivek Kulkarni <vivek_kulkarni@redwood.inference>
To: marissa_cole <marissa_cole@redwood.inference>, Emily Carter <emily.carter@sterlingbank.com>
Cc: rishi_malhotra@redwood.inference, grace_oconnor@redwood.inference
Date: 2026-10-06T13:45:00-04:00
Subject: Re: Failover acceptance, data-lag matrix and timebox discussion

Looping in a couple of operational details Emily asked about that we should call out in the acceptance matrix so your ops team can evaluate recovery risk: 

- Model load strategy: For hosted customers we keep model binaries cold on disk in the standby region but allocate pre-warmed GPU slices per policy. For Dedicated customers we maintain pinned model replicas in standby GPUs (reduces load time to <30s).

- Persistent storage failover: State (logs, customer-provided model artifacts) is replicated to multi-region S3 with cross-region replication. During the run we'll validate object replication lag; typical lag under normal load: <10s. We'll provide replication metrics from the run as evidence.

- Canary & ramp: We propose a three-stage ramp during the test: (1) control-plane failover + health checks, (2) 10% traffic shift + 5min observation, (3) full traffic shift. Each stage will have clear pass/fail gates in the spreadsheet.

- Quiesce: For customers that need strict RPOs for in-flight sessions, we support an optional quiesce window (30s) to flush critical session state to durable storage prior to cutover — we should capture whether Sterling will require that.

I attached a short playbook extract to illustrate the cutover steps. If Sterling wants the Dedicated SLA target (60s) we need a signed reserved-capacity addendum in the contract before the test.

Vivek
Head of Product Ops, Redwood Inference

--

From: Emily Carter <emily.carter@sterlingbank.com>

Cc: technical.ops@sterlingbank.com, procurement@sterlingbank.com
Date: 2026-10-07T17:22:00-04:00
Subject: Re: Failover acceptance, data-lag matrix and timebox discussion

Marissa / Vivek — this is very helpful, thank you. A few follow-ups so we can finalize the acceptance matrix and procurement checklist: 

1) We will accept the 3-minute 95th-percentile RTO for hosted as long as you provide the post-test run report and the evidence bundle (replication metrics + run logs). Please mark that in the matrix.
2) We want the quiesce option enabled for our production run — please include the optional 30s quiesce checkbox in the spreadsheet and outline what actions Redwood will take during that window (flush audit logs, checkpoint control-plane state).
3) For the Dedicated SLA (60s control-plane + 120s routing), we will discuss reserved capacity addendum separately with procurement, but please include the SLA text in the matrix for our internal review.
4) Sandbox run profile: start at 5 rps, step to 25 rps over 10 minutes, hold for 10 minutes, step to 100 rps for 5 minutes, then stop. We'll provide the list of endpoints by Monday.

If you can send the finalized one-page acceptance matrix (with checkboxes and the quiesce option) by EOD Monday 2026-10-11, Procurement will attach it to the contract package. We'll plan the dry-run for 2026-10-13 as proposed.

Thanks again — Emily
